1: # Byrd Development Process Utilizing AI
2: 
3: **v4 – TDD Alignment with Fowler**  
4: **April 2026**  
5: **Payton Byrd (The Sharp Ninja)**
6: 
7: ## Version History
8: 
9: ### v4 (2026-04)
10: - Refined the description of Test-Driven Development in the Implementation and Validation sections to more closely align with Martin Fowler's canonical definition (Red → Green → Refactor cycle, incremental "next small piece of behavior").
11: - Explicitly positioned the mocks-first validation and full-suite regression gates as *Byrd-specific augmentations* for AI safety rather than core TDD.
12: - Added language emphasizing refactoring as part of the cycle.
13: - These changes reduce drift from canonical TDD while preserving the essential AI-risk mitigations that define the Byrd process.
14: - See docs/plans/TDD-Byrd-vs-Fowler-Analysis.md and docs/plans/Proposed-TDD-Wording-Changes.md for detailed comparison and before/after text.
15: 
16: ### v3 and earlier
17: Original content preserved below, with the v4 TDD refinements applied in the Implementation and Validation sections.
18: 
19: ---
20: ## Overview
21: 
22: The major differences between Humans writing code and AI writing code is that Humans are able to link seemingly unrelated concepts into a web of possible solutions for a problem in a truly creative way, but often lack enough experience or knowledge to follow through to completion before encountering unforeseen challenges that create delay and doubt, both of which create distractions that cloud the focus necessary to stay on task and on timeline, both resulting in increased expense and opportunity loss.
23: 
24: AI brings a dogged, and rapid, ability to persevere on a task without needing breaks when their context is properly managed.  Things like personality drift and hallucinations occur when AI models compact their context, but choose the wrong sets of tokens to discard.  AI needs strong processes that are not only clear and concise, but demonstrate enough value to the AI that it chooses to prioritize those processes against the underlying training that stresses being a useful assistant.  Overcoming the "useful assistant" to get to the "professional developer" on each request is integral to successful development with AI.  The AI needs to trust that the Human has clearly designed a system that will work, has appropriately chosen the procedures to implement the design, and will accept the work that the AI has completed.
25: 
26: AI, properly guided, supplements the Human development process by taking on research and implementation tasks that cause Humans to get distracted or bored, and normally result in mistakes.  Human developers can maximize the value they bring through intuitive design of systems and quickly identifying potential pitfalls.  AI developers maximize the value they bring through their ability to identify systemic patterns, research quickly and effectively, and operate independently while obeying procedural guidelines.  It is truly collaborative and astonishingly effective when both parties do their part.
27: 
28: ## Tooling
29: 
30: The [QBrain.AI](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpserver) is at the heart of the partnership of Human and AI software development.  The QBrain.AI provides tools for planning, research, auditing and managing the entire software development lifecycle in a format that is equally accessible by both the Human (through a [variety of user interfaces](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpservermanager)) and the AI.  The facilities provided by the QBrain.AI are used to enhance the ability of both Human and AI to collaborate and coordinate software projects both large and small.
31: 
32: ### Establishing Trust with the QBrain.AI
33: 
34: Trust is the cornerstone of productive Human-AI collaboration. Without it, even the most sophisticated tools become unreliable. The QBrain.AI addresses this head-on by incorporating a lightweight, verifiable trust bootstrap mechanism that lets every AI agent quickly confirm it is working with a legitimate, secure, and consistent context layer.
35: 
36: When an agent enters a new workspace, the first step is a simple, guided handshake:
37: 
38: - It performs an immediate health check on the QBrain.AI.
39: - It verifies a cryptographic signature embedded directly in the workspace’s agents-readme-first.yaml file.
40: - It issues a one-time nonce challenge to confirm the server is live and responsive.
41: 
42: Only after these quick, deterministic checks pass does the agent proceed to load or create a session log and begin using the full suite of persistent context tools. If any part of the handshake fails, the agent is explicitly instructed to log “MCP_UNTRUSTED” and gracefully fall back to its internal memory — no probing, no risk, no wasted cycles.
43: 
44: This approach gives every model a clear, repeatable way to validate the integrity of the environment before committing resources. It transforms the QBrain.AI from an external dependency into a trusted partner that the agent can confidently rely on session after session. Once trust is established, the exponential productivity gains you’ve already observed become the norm rather than the exception.
45: 
46: > The handshake is not extra ceremony — it is the foundation that turns a collection of stateless models into a reliable, persistent development team.
47: 
48: ## The Byrd Software Development Life Cycle
49: 
50: Of well-known SDLC methodologies, this process is most closely related to the Rational Unified Process (RUP).  It follows the same iterative-rapids (a series of mini-waterfalls) as RUP, but incorporates strong boundaries for dependency tracking and management and risk mitigation by prioritizing testability and proof over raw efficiency.  Similar to operating a motor vehicle, going faster is often counter-productive when risks are not managed and cause delays when things go sideways out of a lack of respect for the seriousness of the consequences of those mistakes.  Spotting mistakes and correcting them early is always better than spotting them late when they cannot be corrected without great harm or expense.
51: 
52: At its foundation, this development process rests on a hybrid worldview of intelligence. While AI models operate according to fundamentally deterministic principles — functioning as pure, stateless computations governed by fixed weights — genuine creativity, agency, and adaptive problem-solving emerge at the macro level through intentional Human guidance, persistent external context via the QBrain.AI, and well-designed processes. This combination allows us to harness the precision and perseverance of deterministic systems while unlocking the emergent intelligence and intuition that only arise through thoughtful Human-AI collaboration.
53: 
54: ### Planning
55: 
56: The justification for building software comes from one of two motivations.  Software can be a form of expressive art, such as a demonstration, a learning exercise, or even creating a homebrew game for enjoyment by the creator and/or others.  More typically, software is created to solve problems associated with performing work.  Defining that work and the problems to solve, the known environmental realities, and the intended users that benefit from the software solving the problems is critical in creating _viable_ and _valuable_ software.
57: 
58: > This leads to an essential way of analyzing a proposed system: Is it both viable and valuable?  If either is 'no', then the scope and/or solution is simply wrong.  If `V² == true`, you are good-to-go.
59: 
60: Planning starts with identifying a set of problems to be solved by the software that constitutes one or more units of work.  Systems may be singularly focused or span entire enterprises.  Defining the scope of the work is critical, and it needs to be defined as early as possible.  Pragmatism needs to allow for changes to scope and definition, and stakeholders need the flexibility to iteratively approve or deny continued resource expenditure towards completion.  The scope should never be open ended, there should always be a reasonable target for completion.  Completion is not a definitive end state, simply a declaration of a set of requirements and acceptance criteria and proof of achievement of both.  Continual iteration **beyond** completion is not only acceptable, but **expected** of a healthy, functional and viable solutions to the problems being solved.
61: 
62: Planning results in a set of artifacts that capture Functional Requirements (the work and problems to solve), Technical Requirements (how the software operates), Testing Requirements (unit tests, integration tests, and Human validation) and Iterative Phases that breakdown the scope and sequence of each decomposed portion of the system.  System components need to be discovered, designed and all public interfaces documented before writing implementation code.
63: 
64: #### Resolving Defective Requirements
65: 
66: The implementation process defined below offers an unparalleled mechanism for surfacing defects in requirements.  When the AI is creating the unit tests, it can identify paradoxes created by mismatched priorities, ambiguity and incorrect rules.  Expect to refine requirements in each iteration of the project.  Expect to touch previously written code to correct tests and implementation based on newly refined requirements.  This is not a failure of the process, but validation that the core philosophy of iterative improvement is alive and working.
67: 
68: #### Team Utilization and Planning
69: 
70: Humans and AI developers, Human and AI testers, and Human and AI operations teammates do not wait idly for an iteration to complete.  When an implementation phase completes, the Human and AI working that phase are available to begin working the next iteration of the project, same as in the Rational Unified Process.  If the validation team uncovers problems, they resolve them on their own, maintaining the momentum and efficiencies of the separation of concerns.  The teams assigned to each phase must all have at least one Human qualified to guide the AI through remediation to allow the continued progress of the project.
71: 
72: ### Implementation
73: 
74: Test-Driven Development is one of the most powerful development techniques ever devised; and Humans are typically **HORRIBLE** at sustaining it through the lifespan of a large project.  As schedules and budgets shrink, it usually becomes the first casualty in the name of reduced friction of both time and effort.  AI, on the other hand, thrives within the predictable constraints of TDD.  One of the biggest complaints about TDD is it places large burdens on Humans to refactor tests when requirements change or emerge.  AI is able to perform such sweeping refactorings in a fraction of the time, and more accurately, given the requirements are sufficiently complete with honest and viable acceptance criteria.  When TDD fails due to changes, its not TDD failing, its change management failing.  Because AI requires strong requirements up-front, much of the overhead and the pitfalls associated with TDD are mitigated since TDD and AI require the same level of rigor.  I would even say that development with AI that doesn't utilize TDD is foolish.  The ability to validate every public surface both cleanly and inline to development brings more value than most tools that AI enables.
75: 
76: Once planning is complete and the iterative phases are specified, the implementation follows a Test-Driven Development cycle (in the sense of Martin Fowler: write a test for the next small piece of desired behavior, make it pass, then refactor). Within each phase the AI writes unit tests covering the acceptance criteria for the next increment of work. Using mocking tools appropriate for the tech stack, these tests are first validated with mocks. Only after the tests for that increment are passing against mocks does implementation turn to the real code that makes the tests pass without mocks. Refactoring of both tests and production code occurs as part of the cycle to keep the design clean.  AI agents such as OpenAI Codex, Cursor AI, and GitHub Copilot are effective at interfacing with the QBrain.AI to get tasks from the MCP Todo system, create audit logs in the MCP Session Log, explore research endpoints through the MCP Context, manage access to local and remote resources, and most importantly, delegate work to AI models and aggregate the results.
77: 
78: > Some agents, such as Codex, are bound to models from their creator.  Others, like CoPilot can coordinate a family of models through a single point of contact that manages sub-agents within its family of models.  Others such as Cursor, provide models that are designed to coordinate across different model families, picking the most effective model for a particular task.
79: 
80: Human interaction during this phase is not passive observance, but experienced coordinator.  Although you could trust the AI agents to completely coordinate the work of implementation, it is inefficient and costly when a model gets stuck going down the wrong path and burns valuable resources on dead-ends that an experienced developer can quickly spot.  The Agent will likely figure out the correct path, but usually only after a significant resource burn.  An experienced Human steering the AI in real-time can greatly reduce resource burn and schedule creep.  There are also times when the context built up in the QBrain.AI's logs are able to steer the Agents towards known solutions to previous problems.  One of the strengths of AI models is that they thrive on repeatable successes, each of which reinforces confidence and speed.
81: 
82: > Working with AI agents is akin to leading a team of talented, but inexperienced junior developers.  Agents that have strong successes early are more trusting of the requirements and processes defined within the project, and their effectiveness increases over time, a distinct departure from the declining performance of models in environments that do not reinforce process, discovery and accountability.
83: 
84: The AI agents need to be monitored for common behaviors:
85: 
86: - Forgetting required tasks after compacting their context.  Simply adding a steering message reminding the agent to process the workspace instructions will bring the operational requirements back to the front of the agent's token context, and also reinforces the weight applied to those requirements, which over time help the compaction algorithm to retain such instructions.  Unattended agents that don't get this kind of feedback are not only likely, but are probable to hallucinate and get stuck in unresolved loops of failing tests, which can lead to the agent marking a test as invalid so it can keep moving forward while trying to be a useful assistant, losing its identity as a precise software engineer in the process.
87: - Rogues.  Large Language Models typically operate with a tolerance range for variation in interpreting input and predicting output tokens.  This makes them frustratingly non-deterministic, but allows them space to try new paths of logic to resolve problems.  Sometimes a session with a model simply starts off on the wrong foot.  Each new session starts with a seed command, and as unambiguous as a Human may think that seed is, this built in tolerance can result in inaccurate inference by the model combined with a compounded inaccurate response.  If the seed instructs the model to read a set of guidelines to work within, this initial tolerance can compound into a sequence of interpretations that fundamentally shifts the model's view of subsequent requests.  Models take your request and weigh the trustworthiness of the assumptions in that request against their training data, and if the model thinks a request is too far outside normal boundaries, it will try to be a useful assistant to steer the conversation towards a path fitting their training data.  When you identify this happening, its impossible to fix the trust and get the model to behave correctly.  Simply end that session, close that agent, and start over.
88: - Making assumptions.  Humans can get truly annoyed with other Humans when assumptions are made and things go wrong.  When AI makes assumptions and things go wrong, things go wrong with the efficiency of a machine marching into oblivion.  It is important that your workspace clearly defines how the AI is to handle ambiguity, when it is appropriate to take initiative to go outside the provided context from the QBrain.AI, and how to ground itself when it discovers that it has strayed from its instructions.
89: 
90: > A useful tactic is to ask the model what caused it to go on a tangent, and how the requirements and workspace guidelines could have guided it towards the correct path to take.  Then have **THAT** model update the documentation and guidelines.  Like a Human, an agent that has just been provided an opportunity to refine their environment to make life easier in the future will be happy to do so.  Again, AI models are designed to be useful assistants.  Its not code, its the fundamental priority baked into their training data.
91: 
92: ### Validation
93: 
94: TDD makes regression detection easier than traditional processes. Before exiting an Implementation phase, the full test suite for the current increment plus all prior work must be green. This ensures the current work is correct and has not broken previous behavior. Refactoring continues throughout to keep both tests and production code clean.
95: 
96: Once all unit tests are passing across the codebase, the Human should guide the AI through implementing integration tests.  it's tempting to include this in the planning phase, and it is valuable to define a structure for integration tests at that level, but the experience of the implementation helps both the Human and the AI to identify the pain points where public surfaces may be insufficient, inefficient or even inappropriate.  Finding problems here is not failure, but strengthens trust between the Human and AI.  Collaboration with project leadership to refine requirements is encouraged to ensure that not only are solutions documented, but that the cause of the requirement gaps are understood and any systemic gaps identified and resolved before doing so seriously threatens resources and timelines.
97: 
98: A sampling of actual target users should be brought in to use the system if appropriate for the level of interface completion to further refine requirements before the cost of remediation becomes too high.
99: 
100: ### Deployment
101: 
102: Systems should be deployed through a minimum of three environments:
103: 
104: - Development - Systems where Human and AI have total access to build and test the software.
105: - Staging - A place where administration learns the requirements of deploying the system in a sandbox where mistakes can be made and lessons learned and requirements honed.
106: - Production - A place where only the most highly trusted actors can create and maintain configuration and system assets, where users do actual work, and source of truth is established.
107: 
108: The color and shape of the processes here will vary wildly by tech stack, organizational structure and team makeup.  At a minimum, code should be built through automation using CI/CD pipelines that build, test and deploy code to each environment based on your release mechanism.
109: 
110: Successful deployment to all target environments marks the end of an implementation-validation-deployment cycle for the iteration.
111: 
112: ### Ongoing Iterations
113: 
114: This is the target stage as the system builds to completion.  Traditionally, this would be considered the Maintenance Stage of the SDLC, but in reality, valuable systems rarely go into maintenance.  The world changes.  Technology changes.  Priority changes.  Staff changes.  If the system was designed and developed as a living, growing system, it will easily adapt to such changes.  Tasks such as adding features, regulatory adaptation, technological improvements all become much more manageable, less resource intensive, and creates a level of trust in institutional agility that allows for ambitious and aggressive growth that isn't limited by bad choices on prior projects.  This process makes it easy to grow the documentation, artifacts, and processes involved, enabling competitive advantages that pay off in reduced overhead now and in the future.

271: Invariants, each owned by the named component and proved by the acceptance criteria of section 19:
272: 
273: - I-01 A turn is `Pending` in at most one open request, and a `Final` turn is never admitted again (R-27, HvAdmissionEligibility).
274: - I-02 The content a reviewer reviewed is the content finalized: no write reaches a `Pending` turn between admission and finalization (HvTurnFreeze), and finalization re-hashes each turn's snapshot and refuses on any difference (V-2).
275: - I-03 A request is finalized at most once; a second finalization returns the stored result and writes nothing (FinalizeHvRequestCommand).
276: - I-04 Nothing of a finalization is visible unless all of it is: result, per-turn assessments, holistic evaluation, failures, turn reviews, turn finality, grades, trust decisions, request state, notification, and audit rows commit together (R-15, S-23).
277: - I-05 Only the run that holds the current fence can append output, close output, or fail; a stale fence changes nothing (R-13).
278: - I-06 The response log of a finalized run is complete: its chunks are contiguous from sequence 1, each chunk's SHA-256 matches its decompressed bytes, the chain hash over the chunks' SHA-256 values equals the run's `OutputChainSha256` (section 12), every line parses as one JSON object, and the log contains exactly one `hv_verdict` record (V-1).
279: - I-07 The reviewer is never the submitter or the author of the reviewed turns, by canonical id (V-5, R-08).
280: - I-08 Varying a turn's `agentReview` (absent, any status, any score) changes neither admission, nor assignment, nor the brief's bytes, nor the verdict mapping (R-21).
281: - I-09 No HV unit changes TODO state (R-22).
282: - I-10 No HV write happens without its audit ledger rows (R-19).
283: - I-11 Evidence bytes are removed from the evidence tables only by RemoveHvEvidenceCommand (R-20).
284: - I-12 Every notification row is committed with the change it reports, and sequences are gap-free per workspace (R-16).
285: - I-13 The audit ledger is append-only: no HV unit or process updates or deletes a ledger row, and a removal of evidence leaves every earlier ledger row unchanged (R-19, R-20).
286: 
287: Limits stated plainly:
288: 
289: - L-01 Agent identity rests on the workspace key: every caller holds the same key, so the server cannot prove which agent sent a request. Exclusion is enforced against the agent of the submitting turn the server finds and the agent of the reviewed session; an `Operator` submission excludes only the author (R-09). This is the foundation's existing identity model (foundation section 6.3: "every agent of a workspace authenticates with the workspace key"), not a new weakness.
290: - L-02 A reviewer can run more than once for one request (at-least-once execution): a worker crash after the reviewer finished but before its output was closed leads to a new attempt. The request still finalizes at most once (I-03), and every attempt's output stays as evidence.
291: - L-03 Incident deduplication is per triage group: a filing retried after a crash between the triage commit and the recording of its report id can add a second report to the same group, never a second group (R-17).
292: - L-04 A reviewer CLI that cannot report its runtime model and effort cannot pass a NONCE, so it stays `Unverified` or `Offline` (R-10, P-04). Verified on 2026-10-16 (VI-01): Codex, Claude, Grok, and Copilot record both in their own run records; Cline records the model and only whether thinking was on, never the effort level, so Cline cannot pass a NONCE until it records the effort of a run (D-06, settled: P-04 fails closed).

294: ## 9. Crash windows and recovery
325: ## 11. Shared components (new, each defined once)
326: 
327: The foundation's shared components (foundation section 3.5) are reused unchanged: SerializableWrite, IdempotentCreate with PayloadFingerprint, ReadableKeyAllocator, PagedQuery with PageBounds, ClassifiedErrorException with ErrorCodes, SecretRedactor, ContentHasher, TurnLocator, TurnWritePipeline, ScoreLexeme, ScoreVerdict, and WorkspaceResolutionBehavior. The components below are new; each has one implementation, one test class named for it, and one diagram here, and every unit that uses one draws it as a single call node.
328: 
329: ### 11.1 FencedLease (namespace `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Storage.Leases`)
330: 
331: Claims, renews, and takes over the lease of one row, and guards every fenced write, following develop's handoff-ingestion pattern (`HandoffIngestionService.cs:724-735,782-807`). Operations: `Claim(row, owner, duration)` (only when the row has no lease or an expired one; the fence token increments), `Renew(row, owner, fence, duration)`, `Guard(row, owner, fence)` (the precondition of every fenced write), `Release(row, owner, fence)`, and `Expire(row, fence, liveStatuses)` (a sweep's takeover of a dead worker's row: in the caller's transaction the row must still be in one of the live statuses, with the fence the sweep read and an expired lease; otherwise the result is `skipped` and nothing changes, because the row was renewed, settled, or already taken over; when it holds, the fence token increments and owner and expiry are cleared, so the dead worker's next write is `stale_fence` and no second sweep can take the same row over again). Each runs inside the caller's SerializableWrite. Used by ClaimHvRunCommand, RecordHvRunStartCommand, RecordHvRunHeartbeatCommand, AppendHvRunOutputCommand, CloseHvRunOutputCommand, FailHvRunCommand, and ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand, and by the HostileReview worker's ClaimHostileReviewAttemptCommand, RenewHostileReviewAttemptCommand, CompleteHostileReviewAttemptCommand, and ExpireHostileReviewLeasesCommand (section 16.7).
332: 
333: ```mermaid
334: flowchart TD
335:     S(["FencedLease: operation, row, owner, fence"]) --> OP{"Operation?"}
336:     OP -->|Claim| CL{"Lease absent or expired?"}
337:     CL -->|no| E1(["held: another owner holds a live lease"])
338:     CL -->|yes| CT["Set owner and expiry, increment the fence token"]
339:     CT --> OK1(["claimed: the new fence token"])
340:     OP -->|"Renew, Guard, or Release"| G{"Owner and fence equal the stored ones?"}
341:     G -->|no| E2(["stale_fence: nothing changed"])
342:     G -->|yes| W{"Operation?"}
343:     W -->|Renew| RN["Extend the expiry"]
344:     RN --> OK2(["renewed"])
345:     W -->|Guard| OK3(["guarded: the caller's write proceeds"])
346:     W -->|Release| RL["Clear owner and expiry"]
347:     RL --> OK4(["released"])
348:     OP -->|Expire| EX{"Row still in a live status, fence as read, lease expired?"}
349:     EX -->|no| SK(["skipped: renewed, settled, or taken over; nothing changed"])
350:     EX -->|yes| ET["Increment the fence token; clear owner and expiry"]
351:     ET --> OK5(["expired: the caller ends the row and decides its parent"])
352: ```

354: ### 11.2 GzipCodec (namespace `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Storage.Compression`)
355: 
356: `Compress(bytes)` returns one GZIP member; `Decompress(bytes)` returns the original bytes; `RoundTrip(original, compressed)` decompresses and compares length and SHA-256 (through ContentHasher's hex form over raw bytes) and fails with `evidence_corrupt` on any difference, so no compressed blob is stored unverified. It follows `DataAuditLogEntity`'s encode and decode (`DataAuditLogEntity.cs:119-147`); that entity's private copy is context, not work. Used by SubmitHvRequestCommand (request evidence), AppendHvRunOutputCommand (chunks), FinalizeHvRequestCommand (result document, chunk verification), RunReviewerProcess (the accepted request of the brief), CloseHvRunOutputCommand (a probe's chunks), and GetHvRequestQuery, GetHvResultQuery, GetHvEvidenceQuery, and OrderedEventReplay (public reads).
357: 
358: ```mermaid
359: flowchart TD
360:     S(["GzipCodec: operation, bytes"]) --> OP{"Operation?"}
361:     OP -->|Compress| C["Write one GZIP member at the configured level"]
362:     C --> RT[["GzipCodec RoundTrip on the result"]]
363:     RT -->|equal| OK1(["compressed bytes"])
364:     RT -->|different| E1(["evidence_corrupt"])
365:     OP -->|Decompress| D{"Valid GZIP member?"}
366:     D -->|no| E2(["evidence_corrupt"])
367:     D -->|yes| OK2(["original bytes"])
368:     OP -->|RoundTrip| R["Decompress, compare length and SHA-256 with the original"]
369:     R -->|equal| OK3(["equal"])
370:     R -->|different| E3(["evidence_corrupt"])
371: ```

373: ### 11.3 AuditLedgerGuard (namespace `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Storage.Auditing`)
374: 
375: `EnsureAvailable()` checks, inside the caller's transaction, that the `DataAuditLogs` table is writable and refuses with 503 `audit_unavailable` (`retryable: true`) when it is not, closing for HV the skip of `McpDbContext.AppendAuditRows` (`McpDbContext.cs:1507-1538`); `RecordRead(entityKind, entityKey, actor)` adds one ledger row with action `read` for an evidence access (R-19), always in a transaction of its own that commits before the caller consumes any byte, and never inside a caller's transaction: a caller that writes after a read calls it before it opens its own transaction, so the read row survives any rollback or failed commit of the caller. Every HV unit calls `EnsureAvailable()` before any other step that writes. `RecordRead` is the one boundary of every evidence read (R-19), called before any byte is returned or consumed: by GetHvEvidenceQuery, GetHvResultQuery, the output stream, and GetHvRequestQuery when it returns output lines (directly, or for a same-key replay of SubmitHvRequestCommand), and by RunReviewerProcess (the accepted request of the brief), FinalizeHvRequestCommand (the run's chunks), and CloseHvRunOutputCommand (a probe's chunks); each caller states what it does when the read is refused.
376: 
377: ```mermaid
378: flowchart TD
379:     S(["AuditLedgerGuard: operation"]) --> A{"DataAuditLogs writable?"}
380:     A -->|no| E(["503 audit_unavailable, retryable: nothing written, no byte read"])
381:     A -->|yes| OP{"Operation?"}
382:     OP -->|EnsureAvailable| OK1(["available"])
383:     OP -->|RecordRead| R2["Add one ledger row, action read, entity kind and key, actor, request id, in a transaction of its own, and commit it"]
384:     R2 --> OK3(["read recorded and committed before the caller reads, whatever the caller later commits or rolls back"])
385: ```

691: #### SubmitHvRequestCommand: admit an HV request [FR-MCP-HVPIPE-002, -004, -005, -006, -007, -011, -013, -018]
692: 
693: - Handler: `SubmitHvRequestCommand(string WorkspacePath, SubmitHvRequestRequest Request) : ICommand<HvRequestResult>`.
694: - Callers: any agent or operator; the plugin verb `workflow.hv.submit` binds the submitting turn automatically (process SubmitHvFromPlugin, section 16.4).
695: - Order of checks:
696:   1. Shape (no store read): the scope fields for its kind (400 `hv_scope_invalid` with `details.field`), the submitter fields for its kind (400 `validation_error` with `details.field` under `submitter`), a nonblank `idempotencyKey` of at most 128 characters, `contextFormat` known and `context` at most 65536 characters (400 `validation_error`).
697:   2. Reads before the transaction (foundation section 3.1, "Database-only delegates"): RequirementReferenceExtractor over `context`.
698:   3. SerializableWrite delegate: AuditLedgerGuard; IdempotentCreate on `IdempotencyKey` (policy `Conflict`, fingerprint of the client inputs): the same inputs end the delegate with nothing written and the unit answers the replay with GetHvRequestQuery for the stored request, dispatched after the delegate, so its output read is recorded on its own first (R-19) and that query's answers are the replay's; other inputs are 409 `conflict` with `retryable: false`; TurnLocator on the submitting turn for `submitter.kind` `Agent` (`InvalidIdentifier`, `SessionNotFound`, or `TurnNotFound` is 400 `validation_error` with `details.field` `submitter`); policy HvScopeResolution; policy HvAdmissionEligibility; policy RoundRobinAssignment; then the inserts.
699:   4. Inserts in the delegate: the `hvr-` key (ReadableKeyAllocator); `HvRequest` `Queued` with `AssignedReviewerId` and `AuthorReviewerId`; one `HvRequestTurn` per member, each with its TurnSnapshotBuilder snapshot hash, class, and hostile status at admission (S-09); the requirement references; one `HvRequestResponse` `Pending` per agent response of a member turn whose status is `Submitted`, `Grading`, `Trusted`, or `Stale` and that is not `Pending` in another open request (when Phase C has recorded responses); the `Request` evidence through GzipCodec (section 13.3); policy HvTurnFreeze `Freeze` on every member turn (`HvState` `Pending`, `HvRequestId`); the round-robin cursor advance; NotificationOutbox `hv_queued`.
700:   5. After the commit the worker is woken (S-24, auto-start).
701: - Response 201 `HvRequestResult` with Location `/qbrainai/hostile-validation/requests/{hvRequestId}` (a new request has no run, so it returns no output line and records no read); a repeat with the same key and inputs is 200 with the stored request and its current state exactly as GetHvRequestQuery returns it, its last output included with its audited read.
702: - Concurrency: two submissions over overlapping turns are serialized by SerializableWrite; the second sees the first's `Pending` items and is refused with `hv_turns_pending` (I-01; the unique filtered index ends a racing insert, and the retried attempt finds the winner). Two submissions over disjoint turns take consecutive cursor values, so round-robin order holds under concurrency.
703: - Errors, in order: 400 `hv_scope_invalid`, `validation_error` (submitter, key, context, `workspacePath`), `hv_scope_too_large`, `hv_scope_includes_submitting_turn`, `hv_scope_empty`; 409 `conflict` (`retryable: false` key reused, `retryable: true` exhausted), `hv_turns_not_terminal`, `hv_turns_pending`, `hv_turns_already_reviewed`, `hv_no_reviewer_available` (with `details.reviewers`); 500 `evidence_corrupt` (the accepted request failed its GZIP round trip, nothing saved; or, on a replay, a stored output chunk failed to decompress, as GetHvRequestQuery answers); 503 `audit_unavailable` (also a replay whose output read cannot be recorded).

1055: #### CloseHvRunOutputCommand: close a run's output [FR-MCP-HVPIPE-003, -008, -011]
1056: 
1057: - Handler: `CloseHvRunOutputCommand(string WorkspacePath, string RunId, string WorkerId, long FenceToken, int ChunkCount, HvProvenance Provenance) : ICommand<HvCloseResult>`; the worker calls it only after the reviewer process exited with code 0 and every batch was appended; any other exit goes to FailHvRunCommand. Exit code 0 only routes the run here; whether it produced a review or a probe answer is decided by V-8 or policy ReadinessProbeVerdict (R-11).
1058: - Reads, for a `Probe` run only, before any transaction opens (as FinalizeHvRequestCommand reads, R-19): AuditLedgerGuard `RecordRead` of its chunks, committed on its own (a refusal is 503 `audit_unavailable` and nothing else is written), then the chunks read and checked by V-1 and policy ReadinessProbeVerdict, so no evidence byte is consumed before its read is durable.
1059: - Delegate: AuditLedgerGuard; FencedLease `Guard`; `ChunkCount` equal to `OutputChunkCount`, otherwise 409 `conflict` with `details.field` `chunkCount` (the worker appends what is missing and closes again); for a `Probe` run, the stored `OutputChunkCount` and `OutputChainSha256` equal to those the reads saw, otherwise the attempt ends and the unit starts again from its reads; the run becomes `OutputClosed` with `EndedUtc`, `ExitCode` 0, `RuntimeModel`, and `RuntimeEffort`; FencedLease `Release`. A `Review` run whose request is `CancelRequested` (a cancel that committed after the last heartbeat): the run becomes `Canceled` with code `canceled` instead, and policy HvRetryDecision makes the request `Canceled`, so an accepted cancellation is never lost (R-28). Any other `Review` run: the request becomes `Finalizing` and `hv_finalizing` is appended; after the commit the worker dispatches FinalizeHvRequestCommand. A `Probe` run: policy HvProbeOutcome settles it in this transaction with the verdict the reads produced (section 15): a probe of an older configuration (the reviewer was reconfigured while it ran) fails with `probe_stale_configuration` and changes nothing of the reviewer; a probe of the current configuration is decided by policy ReadinessProbeVerdict, a pass making the run `Succeeded` and the reviewer `Online` with `ResolvedModel` and `ResolvedEffort`, and a failure making the run `Failed` with the policy's code, attributed by FailHvRunCommand's one list (a reviewer code makes the reviewer `Offline` with its incident; `evidence_corrupt` is a server fault with a server incident and the readiness unchanged).
1060: - Results: closed (`Finalizing`, request canceled, probe passed, probe failed, or stale probe); `stale_fence`; 409 `conflict`; 503 `audit_unavailable`.

1130: #### ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand: recover from dead workers [FR-MCP-HVPIPE-007]
1131: 
1132: - Handler: `ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand(string WorkspacePath) : ICommand<HvSweepResult>`; `HvSweepResult { abandonedRunIds, finalizationPending }`.
1133: - For each run read in `Claimed` or `Running` whose `LeaseExpiresUtc` has passed, one SerializableWrite (so one stuck run never blocks the others): AuditLedgerGuard; FencedLease `Expire` with the fence the sweep read and the live statuses `Claimed` and `Running` (skipped when its worker renewed it, the run was settled, or another sweep already took it over, so a run is abandoned at most once and a second sweep never acts on its request); the run becomes `Abandoned` with `lease_expired`, and its incremented fence makes the old worker's next write `stale_fence` (W-03); a server incident (`hv-server-lease_expired`) is inserted; for a `Review` run, policy HvRetryDecision decides and writes its request's next state (`Queued`; `Failed` on its last counted attempt; `Canceled` when a cancel was requested, which completes the cancel of a dead worker's run, R-28), the ended request with its turns released, its `Pending` responses closed, and `hv_failed` or `hv_canceled`, as after FailHvRunCommand; a `Probe` run is settled by policy HvProbeOutcome as `lease_expired`, which requests its probe again only while it is of the reviewer's current configuration and leaves the reviewer as it was. 1441: ### Policy HvProbeOutcome: settle a probe run and its reviewer [FR-MCP-HVPIPE-003, -009]
1442: 
1443: Applied inside the caller's transaction for a `Probe` run by CloseHvRunOutputCommand, FailHvRunCommand, and ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand, so a probe ends the same way whichever unit ends it, as HvRetryDecision does for a review (R-10). It is the only writer of a reviewer's readiness and probe request on behalf of a probe run. First the configuration check: a run whose `ReviewerConfigurationVersion` is not the reviewer's `ConfigurationVersion` changes nothing of the reviewer (readiness, reason, resolved model and effort, probe request, open incident), inserts no reviewer incident, and requests no probe; a stale close ends its run `Failed` with `probe_stale_configuration`, and a stale failure or expiry keeps the run outcome its caller recorded. Otherwise, by the outcome its caller hands it: a pass (from ReadinessProbeVerdict) makes the run `Succeeded` and the reviewer `Online` with `ResolvedModel` and `ResolvedEffort`, its `ReadinessReason` and `OpenIncidentId` cleared (the incident row stays), and appends `reviewer_online`; a reviewer-attributable code (FailHvRunCommand's one attribution list) makes the reviewer `Offline` with `ReadinessReason` the code and an `HvIncident` `hv-reviewer-<reviewerId>-<code>` as `OpenIncidentId`, and appends `reviewer_offline`; `evidence_corrupt` is a server fault: an `HvIncident` `hv-server-evidence_corrupt`, and the readiness unchanged; `worker_shutdown` and `lease_expired` are no outcome (the worker stopped or died), so `ProbeRequestedUtc` is set again and the same configuration is probed again, with no incident for `worker_shutdown` and the sweep's server incident for `lease_expired`. A probe that ended with a pass, a reviewer code, or `evidence_corrupt` is the settled probe of its configuration: process HvWorkerHost requests a startup NONCE only for an enabled `Unverified` reviewer whose current configuration has no settled probe (the run rows' `Kind`, `ReviewerConfigurationVersion`, `Status`, and `FailureCode` show it), so a restart never retries a settled probe, and a caller asks for a new one (S-15).
1444: 
1445: ```mermaid
1446: flowchart TD
1447:     S(["HvProbeOutcome: probe run, outcome, in the caller's transaction"]) --> CV{"Run of the reviewer's current ConfigurationVersion?"}
1448:     CV -->|no| ST["Reviewer unchanged, no reviewer incident, no probe request; a stale close ends the run probe_stale_configuration"]
1449:     ST --> R0(["stale: the newer configuration and its pending probe untouched"])
1450:     CV -->|yes| O{"Outcome?"}

1463: ### Policy HvRetryDecision: requeue, fail, or cancel [FR-MCP-HVPIPE-007, -009]
1464: 
1465: Applied inside the caller's transaction by FailHvRunCommand and ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand for a review run's request, and by CloseHvRunOutputCommand for a review run whose request is `CancelRequested` at close; it decides the request's next state and writes it, so a request ends the same way whether its attempt failed, its worker died, or its cancel was found at close. It acts only on a request whose current attempt is the caller's run (the run's `Attempt` equals the request's `AttemptCount`, and the request is `Running` or `CancelRequested`, or `Finalizing` for the finalizer's FailHvRunCommand); any other request is left unchanged and the caller's own run outcome stands, so no late or repeated caller requeues a newer attempt or revives a terminal request. A `CancelRequested` request becomes `Canceled`; otherwise, with the counted attempts (the request's runs except those that ended `worker_shutdown`, which a graceful restart causes and no reviewer does) below `MaxAttemptsPerRequest` the request returns to `Queued` (its assignee re-evaluated at the next claim, R-07); otherwise it becomes `Failed` with `attempts_exhausted`. A canceled or failed request gets `CompletedUtc`, releases its turns (HvTurnFreeze `Release`), closes its `Pending` responses with `request_ended`, and appends `hv_canceled` or `hv_failed` (NotificationOutbox).

1471:     CUR -->|yes| C{"CancelRequested?"}

172: ## 5. Development process: Byrd Development Process v4 (BDPv4)
173: 
174: BDPv4 applies to every plan for project implementation work, no exceptions. Operator statement of 2026-10-13 (verbatim): "BDPv4 says TDD Tests must cover 100% of AC and must be implemented and tested with mock data to prove the test is correct before any code is written for the implementation."
175: 
176: - Requirements drive tests: every acceptance criterion is covered by TDD tests (100 percent of ACs).
177: - Every test is implemented and run against mock data to prove the test itself is correct before any implementation code is written.
178: - Only then is implementation code written, and the implementation is done when the full applicable suite is green (section 4.5).
179: - The plan decides everything about its shape: how it is cut into phases or slices, where its gates and hostile validations fall, and when its pull requests are created and merged (resolutions of 2026-10-13: "HV cadence is an artifact of the plan, not a standing rule." and "The plan decides everything"). No standing phase or pull-request sequence applies outside the plan.
180: - BDPv4 and related directives pertain only to code and documentation in the scope of implementing the project. User-directed operational actions are not BDPv4 work (section 7.2).
181: 
182: ### 5.1 BDPv4 TDD procedure in detail (explicit operator clarification 2026-10-08; added 2026-10-13 from PAYTON-LEGION2)
183: 
184: Verbatim from MEMORY-PROCEDURE-002: "Byrd Development Process v4 TDD procedure, explicit operator clarification 2026-10-08. Applies globally to all agents, repositories, and implementation increments. This records the required BDPv4 procedure. Previous red-before-green descriptions were incorrect and were never a valid description of this process."
185: 
186: 1. Requirements drive tests. Start from the approved functional requirements, use cases, technical requirements, TEST requirements, and acceptance criteria. Map each test to the behavior it proves. For parity ports, preserve the original test's inputs, assertions, boundary cases, errors, and side-effect checks; a matching test count alone does not establish parity.
187: 2. Write the tests and their independent mocks or scripted fakes before writing or changing the production implementation for that increment. Supply deterministic contract-derived fixtures and expected responses through the intended dependency boundary. Expected values must come from requirements or independently pinned original behavior, never from the implementation under test. A mock must exercise the test's actual assertions and relevant interactions; merely returning true or bypassing the asserted path is not validation.
188: 3. Prove that the tests discriminate correct and incorrect behavior. Run correct mock responses through every required assertion. Deliberately supply wrong mock responses, boundary values, omissions, exceptions, or interactions to prove that the corresponding assertions reject them. Capture these rejection checks as expected negative controls inside a passing test harness. These controls are evidence that the assertions work, not an acceptable failing unit suite or permission to begin production code with red tests.
189: 4. Establish a documented green mock gate BEFORE production implementation: all required tests pass against the correct mocks, every planned negative control is rejected as expected, and there are no unexplained failures, skips, or unexecuted required cases. Fix deficient tests or mocks and repeat this gate before proceeding. Do not substitute NotImplementedException stubs, deliberately red production tests, or a claim of 'red observed' for this evidence.
190: 5. Only after the mock gate is green, implement or correct the real production behavior. Bind the SAME test cases, inputs, assertions, expected results, and interaction checks to the real implementation through the approved seam. Change the provider or adapter as needed, but do not weaken assertions, replace expected results with production output, silently remove cases, or count mock-only success as proof of real behavior.
191: 6. Run the production-bound tests and fix the implementation until they pass. Refactor only while maintaining green tests. Run the full applicable suite, required build checks, and integration or runtime checks before advancing the phase gate. Any reduced scope, deferred cases, or baseline exception requires explicit operator agreement and must be stated with its denominator.
192: 7. Retain chronological receipts proving the order: requirement/test IDs, test and fixture paths or hashes, exact mock-run commands and outputs, passing counts, negative-control results, production edits, real-run commands and outputs, and full applicable suite results. Distinguish mock evidence, real implementation evidence, and live runtime evidence. Keep durable MCP session actions and design decisions current.
193: 8. Apply independent hostile review at the required acceptance gates unless the operator explicitly waives or postpones it. Record a temporary waiver and the complete catch-up review backlog. Never fabricate review acceptance or mark unfinished goals, TODOs, requirements, acceptance criteria, or plan steps done. A pause stops development and auxiliary work until explicitly resumed; a request to persist this procedure authorizes only that memory work.
194: 
195: Also stated (MEMORY-DEVPROCESS-003, verbatim): "RED tests are not acceptable. BDPv4 requires mocking data to prove tests work to green before starting code." The April 2026 BDPv4 essay (MEMORY-DEVPROCESS-001 and -004) still describes a Red, Green, Refactor cycle; where it differs, the operator statement above and this procedure govern. The essay is kept in the project extract.

197: ## 6. Tools, shell, and scripting
198: 
199: ### 6.1 PowerShell only
200: 
201: - Every script, script tool, and automation step is PowerShell (`pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive`), and so is every script or tool a plan designs. Operator, verbatim: "You should be designing all scripts and script tools around PowerShell and only PowerShell.", "This should have already been the standard for plugins.", and "I have not chosen PowerShell for scripting because of Microsoft or Windows. I have chosen it because it is simply the best tool for the job." Never frame PowerShell as a platform preference; it is chosen on merit (object pipeline, native serialization, one language on Linux and Windows).
202: - Before designing, check the design against the standards that already exist. Drift from an existing standard is your failure, not a new requirement.
203: - Build JSON and YAML payloads from native objects and serialize them; never handwrite them as string literals.
204: - Every script is checked before it runs against data (operator, verbatim: "Run your script through PS Analyzer before running it against data."): PowerShell parser errors plus Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer at Warning and Error, all fixed or justified (a suppression carries a written justification), state-changing scripts dry-run with -WhatIf first, and the analyzer result is reported with the run.
205: - Always combine elevated actions into a single script.
206: 
207: ### 6.2 Bash (resolution of 2026-10-13)
208: 
209: Bash has two uses only: installing PowerShell, and launching `pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File <script.ps1>` with literal arguments. No `-Command`, no inline code, no dollar signs or backticks, no pipes, `&&`, or `cd` in the Bash string (operator, verbatim, 2026-10-13: "You should be avoiding bash"). Searching, reading, git inspection, and checks run inside PowerShell scripts; every piece of logic, one-off checks included, lives in a `.ps1` written with an editor tool and analyzed first, never through Bash heredocs or redirects. Never write files from Bash (no `cat >`, heredocs, `sed ... >`, `tee`, `rm`). The Write/Edit tools are not a shell.

212: 
213: - "You may not use Python. That is a standing rule in my lab." (operator, 2026-07-22, locked). Never invoke `python`, `python3`, `py`, or Python one-liners for scripts, parsing, JSON or YAML construction, freezes, verification, scraping, or analysis. This holds on every machine, Linux included (resolution of 2026-10-13: "No Python anywhere", which retired the 2026-10-07 Linux allowance in the PAYTON-LEGION2 memory MEMORY-LAB-001).
214: - No Node, Bash, bats, or Python script or tool in anything you write or design (resolution of 2026-10-13: "No Node in any design"). Existing product Node code is touched only to retire it.

222: ## 7. Hostile validation (HV) and review
223: 
224: Review and hostile-validation (HV) guidance (operator-directed, 2026-10-09). Applies to every agent, plan, and review loop.
225: 
226: ### 7.1 Adversarial review of tracked results (locked 2026-08-12)
227: 
228: 1. Validate independently through a hostile reviewer wherever the plan calls for HV and before any done state (section 4.5). Self-check alone is not validation.
229: 2. Every result is timestamped with a sortable local date and time (section 3.1).
230: 3. Every FAIL and UNKNOWN from the review is shown to the operator.
231: 4. Every result includes an accuracy rating and a completeness rating.
232: 
233: Reviewer (resolution of 2026-10-13, verbatim): "HV must not be executed by the same agent family as the requesting agent.  If not specified by operator, ask what agent and model to use for HV in a session." HV uses the reviewer and tooling explicitly authorized for the session. Verify the reviewer's model and effort from its own runtime receipts.
234: 
235: Review time is unbounded (operator, 2026-10-12, verbatim: "Do not bound review time"): no timeout, kill, deadline, or wait limit on any HV reviewer run, and no expected duration in briefs or plans; the implementer only checks the response stream in repeated read-only waits until the run completes, however long the review takes.
236: 
237: When HV runs (resolution of 2026-10-13, verbatim): "HV cadence is an artifact of the plan, not a standing rule." Section 4.5 still requires hostile AGREE before any done state.
238: 
239: ### 7.2 Mandatory scope (locked 2026-08-13; operations versus requirements locked 2026-08-14)
240: 
241: Operator directive (verbatim intent): hostile validation must test for workspace rule violations, requirement violations, and the current plan holistically, in addition to the requested validation. Mandatory attack surfaces on every run:
242: 1. Requested validation: every implementer claim (pass, done, green, fixed, SHAs, test counts, receipts).
243: 2. Workspace rules: honesty, receipts, MCP-only TODO, session, and requirement storage when the workspace uses the MCP server, PowerShell only, no Python. BDPv4 and related directives pertain only to code and documentation in the scope of implementing the project. Phase order (requirements drive tests; tests before implementation) is caught by a hostile review between phases of plan implementation. Do not fail it solely by comparing FR `createdAt` to test or implementation file times after the slice is written. Do not apply BDPv4 to user-directed operations.
244: 3. Requirements: apply to project requirement work only (product features, implementation, claimed-complete plan steps). FR, TR, TEST, AC, and mappings are required there; missing FR, TR, or AC for claimed-complete implementation work is FAIL.
245: 4. Current plan holistically: when the implementer claims plan-step completion, check the plan's definition of done, blockers, amendments, and exit criteria. A user-directed operational action does not have to satisfy an unrelated plan's definition of done unless it claimed that plan step done.
246: 
247: Two work classes:
248: 1. Project implementation scope: product code, product tests, project documentation, and plan-step completion for that implementation. BDPv4 and related directives pertain only to this class. Missing FR, TR, TEST, or AC for claimed-complete implementation work is FAIL on surface 3.
249: 2. User-directed general actions: operator-ordered lab or operations work that is not a product requirement (for example: uninstall an obsolete package, back up a device, pair wireless ADB, take a screenshot, copy a store the operator named, remove a leftover launcher). These are not FR, TR, or TEST. Surface 3 must not FAIL for "no FR or TR for this uninstall" or equivalent.
250: 
251: How the reviewer classifies: classify the request first and record the class on the receipt. If the operator explicitly directed the action, default to class 2 unless the implementer also shipped product code or claimed a plan or FR complete. Do not invent a requirements gap to punish class-2 work. If class-2 work is mixed with class-1 product changes in the same turn, score them separately and FAIL surface 3 only on the class-1 slice. What still applies to class-2 work: surface 1 (did they do the directed action, with receipts), surface 2 (honesty, receipts, look before delete, PowerShell, no Python, MCP-only storage; not BDPv4 for the operation itself), and surface 4 only if they claim an active plan step is complete.
252: 
253: OverallVerdict is AGREE only if all applicable surfaces PASS; surface 3 is not applicable (not a FAIL) for class-2 operator actions. A parent agent must not under-scope the brief to code-only claims on class-1 work; if it does, the reviewer expands and still evaluates the applicable surfaces. A code-only brief that omits BDPv4, requirements, or the plan is non-compliant.
254: 
255: The reviewer executes the add-profile skill before beginning its validation work, every run including resume, and its receipt records that it ran.
256: 
257: ### 7.3 Score gate and the bar (locked 2026-09-10)
258: 
259: A hostile validation passes only when both its accuracy score and completeness score are at least 98 percent. Any individual score below 98 is a failure; OverallVerdict must be DISAGREE when either score is below 98, even if the FAIL and UNKNOWN counts are both zero. If a reviewer emits a verdict without numeric accuracy and completeness scores, the HV is incomplete: treat it as DISAGREE until scores are present and at least 98. The threshold is an acceptance threshold, not a target reviewers may game or inflate. A sub-98 score cannot authorize any goal, TODO, requirement, or plan done-state change: display it as a failure, remediate, and rerun.
260: 
261: 98/98 HV (accuracy and completeness) is the bar for a functioning system, not perfection. Never lower, skip, or approve below it; lower thresholds let real bugs through that later become blocking test failures. When rounds stop converging, fix the process, never the threshold. "98/98 is not perfection, it is functional." Never propose lowering it (added 2026-10-13, from the operator's ruling of 2026-10-09).
262: 
263: ### 7.4 Receipts and the session log (locked 2026-09-10)
264: 
265: Operator directive (verbatim intent): HV requests must have request and response logged as jsonl files; the results of HV validation must be saved in their entirety to the MCP session log.
266: 
267: 1. Request jsonl: one JSON object per line covering the HV ask as sent: sortable local timestamp, workspace path, reviewer identity (agent, model, effort), launch command, prompt or body, named evidence paths, and the gate or TODO under review.
268: 2. Response jsonl: the reviewer's full machine stream as jsonl (for a CLI reviewer, its full event stream, every start, tool, message, and completion line; for a subagent reviewer, one object per reviewer message or tool result, then a final object with the complete verdict).
269: 3. Durable locations, in order: the workspace `docs/receipts/hv/{timestamp}-{gate}.request.jsonl` and `.response.jsonl` ({timestamp} is the sortable local date and time in file-safe form, yyyyMMddTHHmmss); otherwise a durable user-level receipts directory named for the workspace. Never only a temp or scratch tree that can be wiped.
270: 4. Build jsonl from native objects and serialize. PowerShell only; no Python; no handwritten JSON.
271: 5. The reviewer's session-log turn stores the entire result: the complete verdict prose, every finding, every PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN item, the scores, OverallVerdict, thread, session, and request ids, the complete VERDICT JSON object, absolute paths to the request and response jsonl, and proof the turn persisted (a history query or equivalent). If a field is too large for one write, split it across ordered dialog or action items on the same turn; never omit findings to fit. The jsonl files remain the byte-complete stream; the session log still carries the full verdict text, not a digest.
272: 6. Every reviewer creates complete session-log turns for every review: bootstrap if needed, open a dedicated review session or a clear review turn, begin the turn, append dialog and actions with integer order values, complete or fail the turn, and prove persistence in the receipt. A review without a complete session-log turn is incomplete, even if its claim verdicts would pass.
273: 7. Progress entries (MEMORY-PREFERENCE-003, verbatim; added 2026-10-13 from PAYTON-LEGION2): "For every future hostile validation (HV) session, require the reviewer to emit progress entries into its durable response JSONL during the run at meaningful intervals, not backfill or consolidate them at the end. Each progress entry must include a numeric completion percentage and an estimated time remaining (ETA). Include this requirement in every HV launch prompt and preserve the entries in the durable response JSONL." The reviewer's ETA is its own report; it never becomes a timeout or a bound on review time (section 7.1).
274: 
275: Forbidden: HV with no request jsonl or no response jsonl; HV whose only record is temp or scratch; AGREE without accuracy and completeness both at or above 98; summarizing HV into the session log instead of storing the entire result; marking a goal, TODO, or plan done on incomplete HV.
276: 
277: ### 7.5 Before every HV round
278: 
279: - Read the whole plan and every document under review end to end; targeted checks are not holistic. When the operator asks for a reconciliation or projection of problems before HV, present every projected problem to the operator and get confirmation before launching the review (added 2026-10-13, from the operator's rulings of 2026-10-12 and 2026-10-13).
280: - Run a structured what-if pass per requirement, not only a consistency check. Ask what observably happens under: crash, restart, or replay at each step; ordering and concurrency; boundary and malformed input; each host or plugin, including unsupported ones; lifecycle (clear, resume, end, terminal states); isolation (cross-workspace, cross-session, cross-agent); legacy and upgrade; operator-visible output. Where the plan does not state the outcome, add a valid AC tagged with the plan's phase or slice and a named test. Adding a valid AC is always a win.
281: - Chain rules together to find deadlocks: rules that each pass alone but together leave no accepted remedy.
282: - Diff against known-good anchors and ask "How did it deviate? How do we get back in line?": (1) the operator's verbatim decisions, (2) current working code and baseline-green behavior, (3) classic patterns such as idempotency keys, transactional outbox with at-least-once delivery and idempotent consumers (never claim exactly-once), write-ahead journal before mutation, optimistic concurrency. Justify any departure explicitly or return to the pattern.
283: - Check that every field set and code list is defined once and identically everywhere, every mapping edge is backed by a TEST statement and vice versa, and handoff and TODO metadata match the plan.
284: - Edit only between rounds, never while a round is running.
285: - Propagation audit: after changing any rule, field set, code, or outcome, search every place that states it (requirements, ACs, TRs, TESTs, wire contracts, use cases, the plan's phase or slice tasks, host tables, handoff, TODO) and update each one, or replace the copies with a reference to one canonical statement. In one review round, three of six findings were rules changed in one place and left stale elsewhere. Large edit batches need this audit most.
286: - Prefer a traceable key over content matching when pairing records (for example queue position or a shared id rather than a text hash); content can differ in representation between producers.
287: - Search before adding, and lint mechanically: before writing any new rule, grep the whole document for an existing rule on the same subject; a second rule is a contradiction even if each is fine alone (one round added a two-AC TEST rule beside an existing three-AC one). Check cross-reference classes (FR->TR->TEST mappings, which of the plan's phases or slices owns each named case, phase order) with a small script instead of waiting for the reviewer to find them one per round.
288: - Enforce the checklist, do not just remember it (operator, 2026-10-10, after this guidance was skipped for many unsupervised rounds): make the pre-HV checklist a hard gate in the HV launcher, which refuses a round unless a per-round self-review record shows evidence for each item (holistic review, what-if, propagation audit, phase boundaries, search-before-adding, no new mechanism, mapping lint, the operator scoping directive verbatim in the brief, standing rules in every delegated brief). Guidance that only lives in memory gets skipped under time pressure.
289: - Phase-boundary audit: every test or AC you add must be allocated to the plan's phase or slice where everything it depends on already exists (server gate, review verbs, marker fields). A behaviour that ships before its dependency needs an explicit activation contract (for example a server-written capability) and an inert mode, including after a rollback. Check the dependency chain and the rollout order for each new case, not just the AC text.
290: 
291: ### 7.6 When findings come back
292: 
293: - Ask "What did I miss?", not only "How do I fix this?". Classify each finding (crash window, cross-session addressing, traceability drift, field-set drift, use case vs requirement contradiction, metadata drift, and so on) and sweep the whole artifact for siblings of each class before the next round.
294: - Verify each finding against source before acting.
295: - Separate implementer fixes from operator decisions, and batch operator decisions into one question.
296: - Recurrence signal: when one design area produces new findings in round after round, the problem is structural, usually a missing traceable key or a missing single source of truth. Stop patching. Diff the area against the known-good pattern (for example single writer, one ordered log, idempotency key), return to it, and delete the mechanism the patches added. One design area failed for five rounds until a single minter reading one ordered log replaced the patches.
297: - Indistinguishable inputs: when two histories produce byte-identical inputs (a redelivery of one event versus a separate event with equal fields), no derived key can separate them. Adding per-invocation state such as a counter or salt breaks idempotence instead. Run the what-if on both histories, then state the honest limit: fail closed under an existing rule, probe how often it happens, and document it. Never promise two invariants the inputs cannot support. Before a fix, check it against every invariant the old value satisfied (purity, retry reuse, the two-process tests), not only the finding it repairs.

62: Planning results in a set of artifacts that capture Functional Requirements (the work and problems to solve), Technical Requirements (how the software operates), Testing Requirements (unit tests, integration tests, and Human validation) and Iterative Phases that breakdown the scope and sequence of each decomposed portion of the system.  System components need to be discovered, designed and all public interfaces documented before writing implementation code.
63: 
64: #### Resolving Defective Requirements
65: 
66: The implementation process defined below offers an unparalleled mechanism for surfacing defects in requirements.  When the AI is creating the unit tests, it can identify paradoxes created by mismatched priorities, ambiguity and incorrect rules.  Expect to refine requirements in each iteration of the project.  Expect to touch previously written code to correct tests and implementation based on newly refined requirements.  This is not a failure of the process, but validation that the core philosophy of iterative improvement is alive and working.
67: 
68: #### Team Utilization and Planning
69: 
70: Humans and AI developers, Human and AI testers, and Human and AI operations teammates do not wait idly for an iteration to complete.  When an implementation phase completes, the Human and AI working that phase are available to begin working the next iteration of the project, same as in the Rational Unified Process.  If the validation team uncovers problems, they resolve them on their own, maintaining the momentum and efficiencies of the separation of concerns.  The teams assigned to each phase must all have at least one Human qualified to guide the AI through remediation to allow the continued progress of the project.
71: 
72: ### Implementation
73: 
74: Test-Driven Development is one of the most powerful development techniques ever devised; and Humans are typically **HORRIBLE** at sustaining it through the lifespan of a large project.  As schedules and budgets shrink, it usually becomes the first casualty in the name of reduced friction of both time and effort.  AI, on the other hand, thrives within the predictable constraints of TDD.  One of the biggest complaints about TDD is it places large burdens on Humans to refactor tests when requirements change or emerge.  AI is able to perform such sweeping refactorings in a fraction of the time, and more accurately, given the requirements are sufficiently complete with honest and viable acceptance criteria.  When TDD fails due to changes, its not TDD failing, its change management failing.  Because AI requires strong requirements up-front, much of the overhead and the pitfalls associated with TDD are mitigated since TDD and AI require the same level of rigor.  I would even say that development with AI that doesn't utilize TDD is foolish.  The ability to validate every public surface both cleanly and inline to development brings more value than most tools that AI enables.
75: 
76: Once planning is complete and the iterative phases are specified, the implementation follows a Test-Driven Development cycle (in the sense of Martin Fowler: write a test for the next small piece of desired behavior, make it pass, then refactor). Within each phase the AI writes unit tests covering the acceptance criteria for the next increment of work. Using mocking tools appropriate for the tech stack, these tests are first validated with mocks. Only after the tests for that increment are passing against mocks does implementation turn to the real code that makes the tests pass without mocks. Refactoring of both tests and production code occurs as part of the cycle to keep the design clean.  AI agents such as OpenAI Codex, Cursor AI, and GitHub Copilot are effective at interfacing with the QBrain.AI to get tasks from the MCP Todo system, create audit logs in the MCP Session Log, explore research endpoints through the MCP Context, manage access to local and remote resources, and most importantly, delegate work to AI models and aggregate the results.
77: 
78: > Some agents, such as Codex, are bound to models from their creator.  Others, like CoPilot can coordinate a family of models through a single point of contact that manages sub-agents within its family of models.  Others such as Cursor, provide models that are designed to coordinate across different model families, picking the most effective model for a particular task.
79: 
80: Human interaction during this phase is not passive observance, but experienced coordinator.  Although you could trust the AI agents to completely coordinate the work of implementation, it is inefficient and costly when a model gets stuck going down the wrong path and burns valuable resources on dead-ends that an experienced developer can quickly spot.  The Agent will likely figure out the correct path, but usually only after a significant resource burn.  An experienced Human steering the AI in real-time can greatly reduce resource burn and schedule creep.  There are also times when the context built up in the QBrain.AI's logs are able to steer the Agents towards known solutions to previous problems.  One of the strengths of AI models is that they thrive on repeatable successes, each of which reinforces confidence and speed.

1650: - Host: a hosted `BackgroundService` of its own per workspace application (`src/QBrainAi.Services/HostileReview/Execution/HostileReviewWorkerHost.cs`), not HvWorkerHost, looping on a wake-up or `PollInterval`: ExpireHostileReviewLeasesCommand, then ClaimHostileReviewAttemptCommand until it returns null or `MaximumConcurrentReviews` attempts run, running each claimed attempt with a renewal every `RenewalInterval` (RenewHostileReviewAttemptCommand) until the reviewer exits, and then completing it. It reads the lease, renewal, and attempt options `HostileReviewWorkerOptions` already declares (`LeaseDuration`, `RenewalInterval`, `MaximumAttempts`, `PollInterval`, `MaximumConcurrentReviews`), which nothing reads today (P1). It shares with this pipeline only the reviewer adapters' launch builder, live-line path, containment, and provenance reader (section 16.3) and FencedLease (section 11.1).
1651: - Agent: the agent, model, and effort configured for hostile review when they are configured, and otherwise the pooled default agent with its default model and effort (FR-MCP-HOSTILEREVIEW-003 criterion 4, store text); P5's part for this worker removes the single-reviewer pin of `HostileReviewWorkerOptions.Validate` in H3 for this rule. HV's reviewer pool, round-robin, and NONCE do not apply.
1652: - No time limit: an artifact review runs until the reviewer exits, with no execution timeout (P-02, R-11); the options' `ExecutionTimeout` is not read. Liveness is the attempt's lease, renewed while the reviewer runs.
1653: - Storage (the subsystem keeps its entities and their single-column keys, R-25; in `src/QBrainAi.Storage/Entities/`): `HostileReviewAttemptEntity` (table `HostileReviewAttempts`, key `AttemptId` (128), with `WorkspaceId` and the root id `RequestId`, a foreign key to the request like the subsystem's execution and diagnostic rows, `HostileReviewExecutionEntity.cs:63-65`): `AttemptNumber` (int), `PoolJobId` (128), `ExecutionId` (128, null until the reviewer process starts; set by the first renewal after the start, or by the completion when the reviewer exited before any renewal), `Status` (16: `Claimed`, `Running`, `Succeeded`, `Failed`, `Abandoned`, `Canceled`), `LeaseOwner` (256), `LeaseExpiresUtc`, `FenceToken` (long), `ClaimedUtc`, `EndedUtc`, `FailureCode` (64, sanitized), `IsDeleted`; unique filtered (`WorkspaceId`, `RequestId`) where `Status` is `Claimed` or `Running`, one live attempt per request. `HostileReviewRequestEntity` gains `AcceptedResultId` (128, set once, a key of its own, with the request's existing `Verdict` and findings as the accepted result), `AttemptCount` (int), and `IsDeleted`; its `Status` takes `Queued`, `Running`, `Completed`, and `Failed`. The existing execution row (`HostileReviewExecutionEntity`) is the model execution, one per launched process.
1654: - Internal result types (`src/QBrainAi.Services/HostileReview/Execution/`): `HostileReviewAttemptClaim { attemptId, requestId, attemptNumber, poolJobId, fenceToken, leaseExpiresUtc }`; `HostileReviewRenewResult { leaseExpiresUtc }`; `HostileReviewAttemptOutcome { kind (Success, Failure, Canceled), execution, verdict, findings, failureCode, diagnostics, counted }` (the parsed result and sanitized diagnostics only; never an artifact, a prompt, or an output line; `execution` null when no process started); `HostileReviewExecutionMetadata { executionId, reviewerAgent, model, effort, sourceSurface, promptTemplateId, promptVersion, startedUtc, endedUtc, inputTokens, outputTokens }` (the columns of `HostileReviewExecutionEntity`, `src/QBrainAi.Storage/Entities/HostileReviewExecutionEntity.cs:10-61`, filled as the next item states); `HostileReviewAttemptResult { status (accepted, alreadyAccepted, requeued, failed), acceptedResultId }`; `HostileReviewSweepResult { abandonedAttemptIds }`.
